title: Tooth notation: FDI & Palmer
blurb: How to name any tooth in two characters: FDI two-digit numbers and Palmer grid notation, for permanent and deciduous teeth.
question: During a check-up the dentist calls out 'one-six, occlusal caries; three-one, fine; and on the child's chart, seven-five has a buccal cavity.' Which three teeth are these, and how would the first two be written in Palmer notation?

teach.h: Every tooth needs a unique code
teach.body: Charts, referrals, lab sheets and radiograph requests must identify teeth without any doubt: treating the wrong tooth is a serious patient safety incident. First, the mouth is split into four quadrants: upper right, upper left, lower left and lower right. Right and left always mean the PATIENT'S. Charts are drawn as if you are facing the patient, so the patient's right appears on YOUR left. The UK uses two systems: FDI two-digit numbers (most software and referrals) and Palmer notation (common on paper charts).

teach.h: FDI quadrant numbers (as you face the patient)
teach.caption: Clockwise from the patient's upper right: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 for permanent teeth, and 5 → 6 → 7 → 8 for deciduous teeth.

teach.body: Each FDI number answers two questions. The first digit says which quadrant. The second digit says which tooth, counting outwards from the midline: 1 central incisor, 2 lateral incisor, 3 canine, 4 first premolar, 5 second premolar, 6 first molar, 7 second molar, 8 third molar. So 16 is quadrant 1 (upper right), tooth 6 (first molar). Always say each digit separately: 'one-six', never 'sixteen', so there is no confusion with other numbers.

teach.caption: Highlighted: 16 upper right first molar, 22 upper left lateral incisor, 37 lower left second molar, 43 lower right canine.

teach.body: Deciduous quadrants run 5 to 8 in the same clockwise order: 5 upper right, 6 upper left, 7 lower left, 8 lower right. There are only five teeth per quadrant, numbered 1 to 5 from the midline: central incisor, lateral incisor, canine, first molar, second molar. So 63 is the upper left deciduous canine and 84 is the lower right deciduous first molar. A first digit of 5 to 8 always means a deciduous tooth; subtract 4 to find the matching permanent quadrant.

teach.caption: Highlighted: 55, 63, 75 and 84. The second digit never goes above 5 in a deciduous quadrant.

teach.body: Palmer notation draws the quadrants as a cross, again as you face the patient. Permanent teeth are numbered 1 to 8 from the midline in every quadrant; deciduous teeth are lettered A to E. The quadrant is shown by which corner of the cross sits beside the tooth, or written in letters: UR, UL, LL, LR. So the upper right first molar is 6┘ or 'UR6', and the lower left deciduous second molar is ┌E or 'LLE'. The American Universal system (1 to 32) is not used in UK practice.

teach.caption: The tooth digit is the same in both systems for permanent teeth. For deciduous teeth, A to E in Palmer = 1 to 5 in FDI.

teach.text: Two classic slips. 1) Quadrants go CLOCKWISE, so 3 is LOWER LEFT and 4 is LOWER RIGHT (not the other way round). 2) Right and left are the PATIENT'S, so on the chart the patient's right is on YOUR left. Read 21 and 12 carefully: 21 is the upper LEFT central incisor, 12 the upper RIGHT lateral incisor.

items: FDI first digit = quadrant: 1 UR, 2 UL, 3 LL, 4 LR (permanent); 5 UR, 6 UL, 7 LL, 8 LR (deciduous).
FDI second digit = tooth from the midline: 1–8 permanent, 1–5 deciduous.
Palmer: quadrant symbol plus 1–8 (permanent) or A–E (deciduous), e.g. UR6 = 16, LLE = 75.
If unsure whether a tooth is deciduous or permanent, check the quadrant number and the system in use before preparing.

summary: You can now decode and write any tooth in FDI two-digit notation for both dentitions, name the quadrants clockwise from the patient's upper right, convert between FDI and Palmer, and avoid the classic left-right and quadrant-order mistakes.

A.q: The dentist asks you to record the upper right first molar using the FDI system. Which number do you write?
A.why: Upper right is quadrant 1 and the first molar is tooth 6, so it is 16.

whyNot.0: 26 is the upper LEFT first molar (quadrant 2).
whyNot.2: 46 is the lower right first molar (quadrant 4).
whyNot.3: 15 is the upper right second premolar.

A.q: A referral letter mentions tooth 31. Which tooth is this?
A.why: Quadrant 3 is lower left and tooth 1 is the central incisor.

whyNot.0: The lower right central incisor is 41 (quadrant 4).
whyNot.1: The upper left central incisor is 21 (quadrant 2).
whyNot.2: The lower left lateral incisor is 32.

A.q: A child's chart lists tooth 55. What does this indicate?
A.why: Quadrant 5 is the deciduous upper right, and tooth 5 in a deciduous quadrant is the second molar.

whyNot.1: The upper left deciduous second molar is 65.
whyNot.2: The upper right permanent second premolar is 15; a first digit of 5 means deciduous.
whyNot.3: The lower right deciduous second molar is 85.

B.q: The dentist asks you to chart a crown on tooth 47. Which tooth is this?
B.why: Quadrant 4 is lower right and tooth 7 is the second molar.

whyNot.0: The lower left second molar is 37.
whyNot.1: The lower right first molar is 46.
whyNot.2: The upper right second molar is 17.

B.q: An old paper chart records a filling on LR5 in Palmer notation. What is the FDI number for this tooth?
B.why: Lower right is FDI quadrant 4, and the permanent tooth digit stays the same, so LR5 = 45.

whyNot.0: 35 is the lower LEFT second premolar.
whyNot.2: 85 is the lower right DECIDUOUS second molar; Palmer uses letters for deciduous teeth.
whyNot.3: 44 is the lower right first premolar, not the second.

B.q: In which order are the permanent FDI quadrants numbered 1 to 4?
B.why: FDI quadrants run clockwise from the patient's upper right: UR 1, UL 2, LL 3, LR 4.

whyNot.0: This runs down the right side first; FDI goes across the top first.
whyNot.1: Numbering starts at the patient's upper RIGHT, not upper left.
whyNot.3: This puts LR as 3; it is LL that is quadrant 3, as the order is clockwise.

C.q: While charting an adult, the dentist points to the upper left third molar. Which FDI number should you record?
C.why: Upper left is quadrant 2 and the third molar is tooth 8, so it is 28.

whyNot.0: 18 is the upper RIGHT third molar.
whyNot.2: 38 is the lower left third molar.
whyNot.3: 27 is the upper left second molar.

C.q: An 8-year-old's chart notes a cavity in tooth 75. A colleague thinks it is an adult tooth. Which tooth is it?
C.why: A first digit of 7 means the deciduous lower left quadrant, and tooth 5 is the deciduous second molar.

whyNot.0: The lower right deciduous second molar is 85.
whyNot.1: The lower left permanent second premolar is 35; quadrant 7 is always deciduous.
whyNot.3: The upper left deciduous second molar is 65.

C.q: The dentist plans to treat tooth 14. Which tooth should you prepare for?
C.why: Quadrant 1 is upper right and tooth 4 is the first premolar.

whyNot.1: The upper left first premolar is 24.
whyNot.2: The upper right second premolar is 15.
whyNot.3: The lower right first premolar is 44.

reteach.title: Read it like an address
reteach.question: Think of an FDI number as a postal address: a street and a house number. Which digit is which, and where does the street start?

blocks.body: The first digit is the street: one of four quadrants, numbered clockwise from the patient's upper right (or 5 to 8 for the baby-teeth streets). The second digit is the house number, and every street starts at the town centre, the midline between the front teeth. House 1 is right by the centre (the central incisor); house 8 is at the far end (the third molar). So 36 means 'street 3, house 6': lower left, first molar.

blocks.caption: 36 is the lower left first molar. 63 would be in the deciduous upper left quadrant: the deciduous canine.

explain.body: As you face the patient, number clockwise from the patient's upper right: 1 UR, 2 UL, 3 LL, 4 LR. Deciduous quadrants follow the same order: 5, 6, 7, 8.

test.q: In the FDI system, which permanent quadrant is number 4?
test.why: Going clockwise from the upper right (1), quadrant 4 is the lower right.

explain.body: The second digit counts out from the midline: 1 central incisor, 2 lateral incisor, 3 canine, 4 and 5 premolars, 6, 7 and 8 molars. Tooth 43 is quadrant 4 (lower right), tooth 3: the lower right canine.

test.q: In tooth 43, what does the second digit (3) tell you?
test.why: The second digit identifies the tooth; 3 is always the canine.

whyNot.1: The quadrant is given by the first digit, which here is 4.
whyNot.2: A third molar would be tooth 8.
whyNot.3: Deciduous status is shown by a first digit of 5 to 8.

explain.body: Quadrants 5 UR, 6 UL, 7 LL, 8 LR, with teeth 1 to 5 from the midline. 63 is the upper left deciduous canine; 85 is the lower right deciduous second molar.

test.q: Which FDI number is the upper left deciduous canine?
test.why: The deciduous upper left quadrant is 6, and the canine is tooth 3: 63.

whyNot.0: 23 is the PERMANENT upper left canine.
whyNot.2: 53 is the upper RIGHT deciduous canine.
whyNot.3: 73 is the lower left deciduous canine.

explain.body: A cross divides the quadrants as you face the patient. Permanent teeth are 1 to 8 and deciduous teeth A to E. The corner of the cross beside the number shows the quadrant: UR 6┘, UL └6, LL ┌6, LR 6┐.

test.q: How is the upper left first premolar written in Palmer notation?
test.why: For the upper left the cross lines sit below and to the left of the number: └4.

whyNot.0: 4┘ is the upper RIGHT first premolar.
whyNot.1: ┌4 is the lower left first premolar.
whyNot.2: 4┐ is the lower right first premolar.
